l4hu-bn-opening: Opening Near 100%: The HU Button's Offense

The HU button (SB) opens the action first preflop and acts last postflop; facing the only opponent, the opening frequency can approach 100% — only a few completely junk hands (like 72o, 83o) fold. Because: the SB tops up 0.5 to see a 1.5BB pot (25% required equity), and any hand versus the BB's wide defense range is near or above that line; and since postflop the SB acts last, holding position, the initiative carries all the way into the later streets. High-frequency opening isn't "playing loose" but "using frequency to squeeze every marginal EV".

The core of button opening is "sizing serves postflop", not "sizing serves the steal". In HU use min-raise (2BB) as the main weapon: the steal bar is low (needs 50% fold rate), the small size makes postflop pot control easier, and a wide enough range covers various boards.
Opening-Size Math: Why Min-Raise Is the Main Weapon

SB min-raise to 2BB math (SB already posted 0.5, investing 1.5BB more; BB posted 1, can fold or complete 1):

Pure steal model (baseline = SB folds directly, the 0.5 dead money already sunk):
If the BB folds → SB collects the existing 1.5BB pot; if the BB calls → SB loses another 1.5BB of increment
EV(raise) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5 (f = BB fold rate)
Break-even: f = 1.5/(1.5+1.5) = 50%

So if the BB folds more than 50%, the SB's min-raise with any two cards auto-profits.
Size comparison: min-raise 2BB → 50%; 2.5BB (2 more) → 2/3.5 ≈ 57.1%; 3BB (2.5 more) → 2.5/4 = 62.5%.

Conclusion: the bigger the size, the higher the auto-profit bar. In HU the open's value is postflop, and the smaller the size the easier pot control.

Why doesn't HU use full ring's "bigger size to steal"? Three points: (1) the real HU BB fold rate versus a min-raise is only about 30%-40%, so pure stealing barely profits — the value is postflop; (2) big sizes are "self-punishment" in HU — the BB's calling range narrows with size, so spending 3BB only buys a stronger calling range; (3) frequency and balance — min-raise lets you open about 80% of hands, and only a wide enough range covers the many postflop boards.

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold Q♦J♦. This is a marginal full-ring tight-position hand, but in HU QJs has about 52% equity versus the BB's wide defense range — min-raise 2BB is the standard open. Postflop you add flush/straight-draw potential to the bonus of having the final word, and QJs on the HU button is an absolute opening hand.

Example 2 (sizing adjusts to the opponent): You observe the BB folds to min-raises at 55%. The min-raise's pure-steal EV = 0.55×1.5 − 0.45×1.5 = +0.15BB (slightly positive, with most profit still coming postflop), and you can raise the open frequency toward 100% because the BB's fold rate lifts steal profit. Conversely, if the BB 3-bets frequently, narrow your range and reduce the marginal hands that only fold after a 3-bet.

Counterintuitive point: the HU button "opening near 100%" isn't greed but math. But note — opening wide doesn't mean investing every street. Postflop, adjust by board fit and let go in time — that's the mature "participate a lot, invest little" play.

Button opening quick check — default min-raise 2BB, opening about 80%-100%; top 15% strong hands + middle suited connectors/Ax + bottom garbage mix. Every 50 hands check two things: (1) are the opponent's 3-bets pushing you out of your opening? (2) is the BB's fold rate high enough to support opening to 100%?
l4hu-ev-adjustments: Heads-Up Pots: EV Calculation Simplified and Amplified

HU has only two-player pots, so EV calculation is simpler than full ring, but the numeric meaning is amplified. Simplified: no multiway splitting, no "one of my outs gives another opponent a flush" dilution — your equity is closer to "equity vs a single range". Amplified: dead money share is high (SB 0.5) and the opponent's range is wide, so the same EV differences are repeated at high frequency in HU, accumulating into bigger long-term returns. Understanding these two changes is the core of HU EV adjustments.
The core HU EV formula is unchanged, but the inputs are clearer: EV(call) = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B. The difference is "wider opponent range, higher dead-money share", turning more marginal calls +EV.
Preflop Steal EV and Postflop Positional EV

Preflop steal EV (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f, baseline = folding directly):
EV(steal) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5 (break-even f = 50%)

Postflop positional EV anchor:
HU positional value about 0.5-1BB/hand (the SB is IP postflop every hand)

Example: BB facing an SB min-raise (SB has 2BB in, the BB already has 1BB in):
General formula: required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent's bet + your call)
Substitute: 1 ÷ (1.5 + 1.5 + 1) = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%
(Current pot 1.5 = SB's 0.5 + the BB's own 1 — that 1BB is dead money yet still belongs in the denominator; opponent's bet 1.5 = SB's increment up to 2BB; your call 1 = the BB top-up. Equivalently the total pot after you call is 4BB, so 1÷4 = 25%)
Marginal hands often have 40%+ vs the SB's ~80% opening range → call is +EV

The practical meaning of HU EV adjustments: against the SB's wide range, the BB's call bar drops sharply. Full ring's 40% call line versus a 15% UTG range drops to 25% in HU versus an 80% SB range (1BB more into a 4BB pot after the call), and against a range as wide as about 80%, marginal hands simply carry more real equity themselves. That's why the HU BB can defend 60%+ — not "loose" but "the result of EV calculation".

Example: HU blinds 0.5/1, preflop the SB min-raises 2BB, you (BB) hold K♠7♠. Calling 1BB makes the total pot SB 2 + the BB's own 1 + your call 1 = 4BB, so required equity = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. K7s has about 48% equity vs the SB's ~80% opening range — a surplus of about 23 points. Postflop you check first and lean on check-calls: a K lets you bet thin value, flush/straight draws chase cheaply, and a complete miss can fold. The call is +EV — full-ring K7s versus UTG is a fold, but HU versus the SB's wide range it's a +EV call.

Example 2 (postflop EV decision): flop pot 4BB — the BB acts first, the SB (IP) bets 2BB (half pot). Required equity to call = 2/(4+2+2) = 25%. Your 76 on a 9♠8♦3♣ board has a double-gutshot + backdoor flush, about 8 outs at 17% single-street — not enough at 25% alone, but adding implied odds (win 2.5BB more when the straight hits) makes the call +EV. HU draw calls rely more on implied odds because the opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness.

Counterintuitive point: in HU "small cards" aren't junk. 9-high can still win postflop in HU — the opponent's calling range is extremely wide, so 9-high's showdown value far exceeds full ring. At the same 25% pot odds, 9-high may be ahead 40%+ of the time in HU vs only 15%-20% in full ring.
HU EV quick anchors: half-pot bet needs 25%, 1/3 pot 20%, full pot 33.3%; limp to see a flop 25%, call a 3BB open 33.3%. Memorize these — faster than counting at the table.
l4hu-gto-basics: Heads-Up: The Purest Application of Equilibrium Strategy

HU poker (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, where the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee strictly holds. This means HU has an equilibrium strategy (GTO): no matter how the opponent plays, your long-term expectation is never below the game value. Compared with full ring, HU GTO ranges are extremely wide (SB opens about 80%, BB defends 60%+), and equilibrium means very high betting frequency and bluff density — GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter".

HU GTO's positioning is a "bulletproof vest", not a "weapon": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. HU pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".
Frequency Baselines: Value:Bluff Ratio and MDF

Equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet (pot P, bet P):
Bluff share f = b/(1+2b) = 1/(1+2) = 1/3
So value:bluff = 2:1.

Half pot (b=0.5): f = 0.5/2 = 25%, value:bluff = 3:1.

MDF (Minimum Defense Frequency) = 1/(1+b):
half pot → 67%; full pot → 50%; 2× pot → 33%.

The HU BB defending 60%+ far exceeds the MDF floor (about 33%-38%) because its preflop final say and dead-money pot odds make calling itself +EV.

The frequency difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO: in full ring most positions can only play tight with low equilibrium betting frequencies; HU has wide ranges, high betting frequencies, and high bluff density. Solvers output lots of aggressive bets and polarized ranges in HU. Understanding these baselines is the prerequisite for recognizing "when the opponent deviates from equilibrium".

Example: in an HU SB-vs-BB solve the solver says the SB opens about 80% and the BB defends about 60%+; postflop the OOP BB checks at high frequency while the IP SB bets at high frequency. These frequencies look "loose" but they are all part of equilibrium — any deviation by one side (e.g. the SB opening only 50%) lets the other exploit it by widening defense or raising steal frequency.

Example 2 (positional symmetry): in HU the two sides swap SB/BB every hand — position isn't fixed: the SB opens the action first preflop and the BB has the final say; postflop the BB acts first and the SB acts last. The GTO equilibrium includes positional strategies for both directions; positional symmetry means you must play both the SB and the BB, not carry full ring's "fixed position" thinking.

Counterintuitive point: "GTO is playing tight" is the biggest misreading. HU GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and thin value — it just keeps all of it at ratios the opponent can't counter. When studying solvers, don't memorize frequencies — ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why is this hand in the betting range? Why did the frequency change on the turn?

HU GTO learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape" (why play this way), then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit.
l4hu-counter-strategies: Identifying Deviations: The Prerequisite of HU Counter-Strategies

The core of HU counter-strategy is: first identify the opponent's deviations from equilibrium, then calibrate with the GTO baseline the optimal response against that leak. The four common HU deviations: folds too much (super-high fold rate vs C-Bets), calls too loose (calling station), 3-bets too often, C-Bets too often. Identification relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics, not single-hand impressions.

The right posture of countering: aim the direction at the opponent's leak (Maximally Exploitative), keep the magnitude minimal (Minimally Exploitative). Every deviation opens your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.
Targeted Counters for the Four Deviations

Raising steals against an over-folding opponent (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f, baseline = folding directly, the 1.5/1.5 basis):
EV(steal) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5

Equilibrium fold rate about 40% (f=0.4) → EV = 0.4×1.5 − 0.6×1.5 = −0.3BB (unprofitable, recovered postflop)
At 60% fold rate (f=0.6) → EV = 0.6×1.5 − 0.4×1.5 = +0.3BB (pure steal auto-profits)
At 70% (f=0.7) → EV = 0.7×1.5 − 0.3×1.5 = +0.6BB (profit grows)

Conclusion: the higher the opponent's fold rate, the more your steal frequency should rise, but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 50%".

The counter directions for the four deviations: (1) folds too much → raise open/C-Bet frequency with more semi-bluffs; (2) calls too loose (station) → cut pure bluffs, switch to value-bet thin value (top pair weak kicker bets for money); (3) 3-bets too often → narrow the open range and add 4Bet value; (4) C-Bets too often → raise x/r frequency and float. Each advances in a "identify → counter → re-check" loop.

Example: You observe a HU opponent who folds to C-Bets at 60% (equilibrium ~45%). That's a clear over-folding leak. Counter: raise your flop C-Bet frequency and bluff density overall, even adding weak hands that originally checked to the betting range. But cap it at "I still don't lose if he tightens to 50%" — this is "using GTO as the baseline and making directed, disciplined deviations from observable biases".

Example 2 (countering a station): The opponent almost never folds postflop (fold rate <25%). Counter: no pure bluffs (he doesn't fold); switch to value-bet thin value — top pair weak kicker also bets for money because he calls with worse. Meanwhile convert bluffs to semi-bluffs or checks. A station is the easiest HU type to extract from, as long as you can resist bluffing.

Example 3 (node locking in practice): In a solver, lock "this opponent folds to turn double-barrels 55%" as a fixed frequency and re-solve your optimal response — the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher. That's node locking turning countering from "feel" into "calculation".

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of countering isn't "countering too little" but "over-countering and becoming the leak yourself". HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel while harvesting — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Counter execution in five steps: (1) HUD-collect enough samples to confirm the leak; (2) lock the node in a solver for the optimal response; (3) compare to baseline and mark the pushed-up frequencies and sizes; (4) execute live; (5) re-check the sample every 500 hands.

options: Narrowing the range, reducing marginal hands that only fold after a 3-bet

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.question: The main difference between HU and full-ring EV calculation is:
options: No multiway dilution, high dead-money share, wide opponent range — the EV numbers are amplified
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q1.explanation: The EV formula is unchanged, but HU two-player pots have no dilution, the SB's dead money share is high, and the opponent's range is wide — turning more marginal calls +EV and amplifying the meaning.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.question: SB min-raises to 2BB (the BB already has 1BB in); the BB still has to call 1BB. Required equity is about:
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q2.explanation: Required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent's bet + your call) = 1 ÷ (1.5 + 1.5 + 1) = 1 ÷ 4 = 25%. The denominator must include the BB's own 1BB already in the pot (1/(2+1) ≈ 33.3% is exactly the value you get by omitting it). HU's dead-money share is high — cheaper than the full-ring BTN call at 40%.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.question: The root reason the HU BB defends 60%+ is:
options: The call bar is low vs the SB's wide range, and the BB's preflop final say adds information
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q3.explanation: Vs the SB's ~80% wide range the call bar drops to 25% (1BB more into a 4BB pot after the call); the BB has the final say preflop and its dead money makes the price cheap, so it can defend wide — the result of EV calculation, not looseness. The over-100% equity-realization bonus belongs to the position-holding SB, not the BB.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.question: HU draw calls (like double-gutshots) rely on implied odds because:
options: The opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness — winning more when the draw hits
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q4.explanation: The HU opponent's range is wide with high payment willingness, so you win more when the draw hits (good implied odds), compensating for the single-street equity shortfall.

l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.question: HU positional value of about 0.5-1BB/hand means:
options: The BB wins 1BB more every flop
Over the long run the SB earns 0.5-1BB more expected value per hand than the BB
l4hu-ev-adjustments-q5.explanation: Positional value is a long-run expectation gap: the SB acts last postflop holding IP, averaging 0.5-1BB extra per hand — a statistical expectation, not a per-hand guarantee.

l4hu-gto-basics-q1.question: The applicability of the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee in HU:
options: Strictly holds (HU is a pure two-player zero-sum game)
l4hu-gto-basics-q1.explanation: HU (ignoring rake) is a pure two-player zero-sum game, where the Nash unexploitable guarantee strictly holds. Multiway pots weaken under coalition effects.

l4hu-gto-basics-q2.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet is about:
l4hu-gto-basics-q2.explanation: Bluff share f = 1/(1+2) = 1/3, so 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. Exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

l4hu-gto-basics-q3.question: The main difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO is:
options: HU ranges are extremely wide with high betting frequencies and bluff density
l4hu-gto-basics-q3.explanation: HU ranges are wide (SB 80%, BB 60%+), so equilibrium comes with high betting frequencies and polarized ranges — not "playing tight".

l4hu-gto-basics-q4.question: Why does the HU BB defend 60%+, far above the MDF floor (about 33%-38%)?
options: The BB has better cards every hand
The BB has the final say preflop, and its 1BB of dead money makes calling cheap
The MDF formula doesn't apply preflop
l4hu-gto-basics-q4.explanation: MDF only guarantees "stopping pure-bluff auto-profit"; the BB's positive call EV comes from having the final say preflop plus its dead-money odds, so it can defend above the floor and still profit. The over-100% equity-realization bonus belongs to the position-holding SB.

l4hu-gto-basics-q5.question: HU "positional symmetry" means:
options: Every hand the two sides swap SB/BB — you must play both the SB and the BB
l4hu-gto-basics-q5.explanation: In HU the two sides swap SB/BB every hand — the order flips (the SB opens first preflop and acts last postflop; the BB is the reverse); the GTO equilibrium includes positional strategies in both directions.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.question: The correct basis for identifying a HU opponent's deviation is:
l4hu-counter-strategies-q1.explanation: HU countering relies on 50-100 hand frequency statistics (fold rate/3-bet rate, etc.); single-hand impressions are noise, insufficient evidence.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.question: Against an over-folding opponent, the correct counter is:
options: Raise open/C-Bet frequency and add semi-bluffs
l4hu-counter-strategies-q2.explanation: An over-folding opponent makes steal and C-Bet fold rates automatic profit — raise open/C-Bet frequency and semi-bluff density.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.question: Against a calling station who calls too loose, the correct counter is:
options: Cut bluffs and switch to value-bet thin value
l4hu-counter-strategies-q3.explanation: A station doesn't fold, so pure bluffs are useless; switch to value-bet thin value because he calls with worse hands.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.question: The discipline of "minimum necessary deviation" is:
options: Aiming at the opponent's leak with minimal magnitude, ready to return to baseline anytime
l4hu-counter-strategies-q4.explanation: Deviations open your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled; aim at the leak, keep it minimal, and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.question: The role of node locking in countering is:
options: Locking the opponent's deviation as a fixed frequency and re-solving your optimal response
l4hu-counter-strategies-q5.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays (deviation)" into the solver and outputs the optimal counter against that bias — turning countering from feel into calculation.
